roadmap.title: Find a room and a problem
roadmap.question: Where do people already build, and what keeps them stuck?
actions: Attend one public builder event or club meeting.
Talk to three people about work they already do; record problems, not solution ideas.
Choose one audience you can reach again next week.
roadmap.exit_signal: One specific audience and three documented pain points.

roadmap.title: Check whether the pain is real
roadmap.question: How often does the problem happen, what does it cost, and what do people do now?
actions: Interview ten people in the same audience; ask about the last time the problem happened.
Write down their current workaround, who owns the budget, and what a fix would change.
Look for repeated behavior, not compliments about an idea.
roadmap.exit_signal: Several people describe the same costly problem without prompting.

roadmap.title: Make the smallest useful test
roadmap.question: Can one person get a result before a full product exists?
actions: Sketch the promised outcome in one sentence.
Deliver a manual, spreadsheet, prototype, or concierge version to one tester.
Watch the tester use it and log where they hesitate.
roadmap.exit_signal: At least one user gets the promised result and asks to use it again.

roadmap.title: Find users and earn the first dollar
roadmap.question: Will a buyer commit time or money for the result?
actions: Write a narrow pilot offer with outcome, price, and delivery date.
Send relevant one-to-one outreach and ask for a short conversation.
Ask a qualified buyer to pay for a small pilot; deliver it and measure the result.
roadmap.exit_signal: A completed paid transaction or signed paid pilot, with the buyer's reason for purchasing recorded.

roadmap.title: Choose capital for the milestone
roadmap.question: What will funding prove that customer revenue cannot yet finance?
actions: Write the next milestone, amount needed, and evidence already collected.
Compare a grant, customer prepayment, campus program, and equity before applying.
Use the official application and current eligibility page for each program.
roadmap.exit_signal: A specific use of funds and a shortlist of programs matched to stage and eligibility.

roadmap.title: Make the result repeatable
roadmap.question: Can another buyer get the result with less founder effort?
actions: Track repeat use, retention, and gross margin rather than only signups.
Document the delivery steps that worked for early customers.
Automate a step only after its manual version has worked repeatedly.
roadmap.exit_signal: Repeat purchases or sustained use in one customer segment.

playbooks.title: Interview people before pitching
playbooks.goal: Learn what people already do, what breaks, and whether the pain is worth solving.

steps.action: Pick one job title or user group; write a one-sentence hypothesis about a recurring problem.
Recruit ten conversations through classmates, campus events, public Purdue contacts, and relevant alumni. Ask for 15 minutes, not a product verdict.
steps.output: Interview list with source and status.

steps.action: Ask: When did this last happen? What did you do? What did it cost in time or money? Who decides to buy a fix?
Compare answers. Keep the problem only if multiple people independently describe the same friction and a plausible budget owner exists.

avoid: Leading questions such as 'Would you use my app?'
Counting praise as evidence of demand.

playbooks.title: Reach out to Purdue alumni and potential buyers
playbooks.goal: Start enough relevant conversations to learn which audience responds and why.

steps.action: Define a narrow recipient: role, company type, problem, and why this person is relevant. Start with public Purdue alumni and program contacts, then expand to buyers outside Purdue.
Build a 30-person research list. Record each person's public source, reason to contact, date sent, reply, follow-up, and outcome. Do not treat the alumni directory as consent for a bulk mailing list.

Send a short personal note with one real reason for contacting that person and one small ask. Test two audience segments over 25–50 individually relevant messages; treat that volume as an experiment target, not a universal benchmark.
Follow up once after several business days with a useful observation or a clear close-out. Stop when asked. Record replies, booked calls, and confirmed problems rather than open rates.
steps.output: Reply and conversation rates by segment.

steps.action: After each conversation, ask who else has the problem and request an introduction only when there is a good fit.
steps.output: Warm introductions and updated audience hypothesis.

templates.subject: Purdue student researching [specific problem]
templates.body: Hi [Name], I'm a Purdue [student/researcher/alum] speaking with [specific audience] about [problem]. I saw your work on [specific public project or role]. Could I ask you two questions in a 15-minute call next week? I'm trying to understand how people handle this today, not pitch a product. Thanks, [Name]

templates.subject: Idea for [specific outcome] at [company]
templates.body: Hi [Name], I noticed [specific public signal]. Teams like yours often spend [time or cost] on [problem]. I can help [specific result] in a [duration] pilot for [price], with [deliverable]. Worth a 15-minute look? If this is off target, no need to reply. [Name]

templates.subject: Re: [original subject]
templates.body: Hi [Name], one more thought: [useful observation or example relevant to their work]. If [problem] is on your list this quarter, I can share what I learned from similar teams. If not, I'll close the loop here. [Name]

avoid: Generic mass mail to every listed alumnus

playbooks.title: Earn the first dollar
playbooks.goal: Get a buyer to pay for a specific outcome, even if delivery is manual.

steps.action: Choose one buyer with a problem already observed in interviews. State the before-and-after result in plain language.
Make a small pilot: fixed scope, delivery date, success measure, and price. For research or hardware, a paid feasibility study can be the first offer.
Show the offer to five qualified buyers. Ask directly: 'Would you pay [price] for [result] by [date]?' Record objections without arguing.
For a yes, use an invoice or a payment link, state the terms clearly, and collect payment or a deposit before expanding scope.
steps.output: Paid order or signed paid pilot.

steps.action: Deliver manually if needed, measure the result, and ask what the buyer would purchase again. Use that evidence before seeking a larger grant or investor check.

playbooks.sample_offer: I will reduce [specific task] from [current effort] to [target] for [buyer] in 14 days. Pilot price: [amount]. Includes [three deliverables]. Success means [observable result].
avoid: Building the entire platform before asking a buyer to pay
Changing price or scope after agreement without consent

playbooks.title: Start a permission-based email channel
playbooks.timebox: One week to set up; review monthly
playbooks.goal: Keep interested people informed without mixing a newsletter with one-to-one research outreach.

steps.action: Decide who the update is for and what they will get, such as a monthly product note or founder event digest. Put that promise beside an opt-in form.
Record how and when each subscriber opted in. Do not import public alumni contacts or cold prospects into a marketing audience without permission.
Send a welcome note with the promised topic, frequency, and a reply question. Include a working unsubscribe path in each campaign.
Send a useful update on a consistent cadence: one finding, one example, one next step. Segment only when interests actually differ.
Review replies, signups, unsubscribes, and purchases. Stop sending content people did not ask for.

templates.subject: You're on the [topic] list
templates.body: Thanks for joining. Every [frequency], I'll send [specific useful content]. This week: [one concrete finding]. What is the hardest part of [problem] for you right now? Reply with one line. You can unsubscribe any time using the link below.

avoid: Treating a public email address as newsletter consent
Buying or scraping a marketing list

glossary.definition: A time-bound program that helps a startup make progress through mentorship, peers, and sometimes capital.
glossary.example: A cohort can be useful after you know the customer problem you are testing.

glossary.definition: An individual investing personal money in a company, often at an early stage.
glossary.example: An angel check may fund a specific next milestone; terms still matter.

glossary.definition: Annual recurring revenue: the annualized value of active recurring subscriptions. One-time sales are excluded.
glossary.example: $1,000 in stable monthly subscriptions corresponds to $12,000 ARR.

glossary.definition: How much cash a company spends net of cash it brings in over a period, commonly per month.
glossary.example: If cash falls by $5,000 in a month, net burn was $5,000.

glossary.definition: Customer acquisition cost: sales and marketing cost divided by the number of new customers acquired in the same period.
glossary.example: $500 spent to acquire five paying customers gives $100 CAC.

glossary.definition: Customers or recurring revenue lost during a period. State which one you mean.
glossary.example: Two of 20 subscribers leaving in a month is 10% customer churn.

glossary.definition: A direct message to someone who has not previously agreed to speak with you, sent because their work is relevant to a specific question or offer.
glossary.example: Ask an alumnus about a problem they publicly work on; do not add them to a newsletter.

glossary.definition: A manually delivered version of a service used to test the promised result before automation.
glossary.example: Create the weekly report by hand for one paying buyer before building a dashboard.

glossary.definition: The share of people at one step who complete the next action you measure.
glossary.example: Five paid pilots from 50 qualified conversations is a 10% conversation-to-pilot rate.

glossary.definition: A founder's ownership percentage falls when new shares are issued to investors or employees.
glossary.example: Raising equity can lower each existing holder's percentage even as company value changes.

glossary.definition: A conversation about a person's past behavior, current workflow, and costly problem before pitching a solution.
glossary.example: Ask 'What happened the last time?' instead of 'Would you buy this?'.

glossary.definition: Revenue remaining after direct costs of delivering the product or service, expressed as a percentage of revenue.
glossary.example: $100 revenue minus $30 direct cost gives 70% gross margin.

glossary.definition: Ideal customer profile: a narrow description of the organization or person most likely to benefit from and pay for a product.
glossary.example: Independent machine shops with 5–20 employees and frequent quote delays is more useful than 'manufacturers'.

glossary.definition: Estimated total value a customer generates over the relationship; early estimates are uncertain.
glossary.example: A $50 monthly customer retained for 12 months yields $600 in revenue before costs.

glossary.definition: Monthly recurring revenue: predictable monthly revenue from active subscriptions, excluding one-time fees.
glossary.example: Ten $20 monthly subscriptions yield $200 MRR.

glossary.definition: Minimum viable product: the smallest version that lets a real user experience the core value and gives the team evidence.
glossary.example: A working form plus manual fulfillment may test demand before a full app.

glossary.definition: A limited, paid engagement to test a promised outcome with a real buyer.
glossary.example: A two-week trial with a defined deliverable and price is a paid pilot.

glossary.definition: Strong evidence that a specific market repeatedly wants and uses a product; there is no single universal numeric threshold.
glossary.example: Customers return, refer peers, and pay again without constant persuasion.

glossary.definition: An estimate of how long existing cash lasts at the current net burn rate.
glossary.example: $30,000 cash divided by $5,000 monthly net burn gives about six months of runway.

glossary.definition: Simple Agreement for Future Equity: an investor funds a company now for the right to shares later under agreed terms; it is not a loan.
glossary.example: A SAFE may convert when the company raises a priced equity round.

glossary.definition: Federal small-business research programs supporting eligible R&D with commercial potential; STTR involves a research institution partner.
glossary.example: A deep-tech team might assess NSF SBIR/STTR before selling equity.

glossary.definition: Observed progress showing people want the solution, such as active use, repeat purchases, or paid pilots.
glossary.example: Three buyers paying for the same outcome is stronger evidence than three verbal compliments.

glossary.definition: The maximum valuation used when a capped SAFE converts to shares in a later priced round.
glossary.example: The cap changes how much ownership an early investor receives at conversion.
